preamble: Monophthongization of the diphthong *ei to a high front vowel [iː]. It took place directly within Proto-Germanic, where the remaining *ei became *ī in the late period (*teiwaz > *Tīwaz, PIE *stéygʰeti > *stīganą 'to climb'), and in Proto-Slavic, where Proto-Balto-Slavic *ei became *ī as part of the general monophthongization of diphthongs (*weiˀdēˀtei > *viděti 'to see'), while Baltic kept a diphthong (Lithuanian veizdėti, žiema). The same outcome in Latin (deicō > dīcō) and post-classical Greek (ει > [i]) passed through an attested intermediate [eː] stage and is therefore a chain, not a one-step change.

examples.note: PIE *ei became Proto-Germanic *ī; Greek στείχω keeps the diphthong.
Late Proto-Germanic eliminated the remaining /ei/, changing it to /iː/.
Balto-Slavic *ei became Proto-Slavic *i; Lithuanian veizdėti 'to look' keeps the diphthong.
Same change; Lithuanian žiema 'winter' (from the same *źeimā́ˀ) shows the Baltic reflex ie.

sources: Wikipedia (2026). History of Proto-Slavic: Monophthongization and other vowel changes. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Proto-Slavic
